clue.text: Hand over a scene describing The Great Dictator?

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so the hand goes round the other letters

parts.note: a clenched hand is a fist
SC is the script abbreviation for scene

explanation.surface: A film question about who hands over a scene in Chaplin's satire The Great Dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: The Great Dictator is Chaplin's 1940 film lampooning Hitler; the question mark flags that the title stands for any such tyrant.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaplin's title character is a parody of Hitler, a model of the far-right tyrant, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Joe's over in a small sports bar serving woman

indicators.note: the reversed soldier is placed inside the cricket bar

parts.note: a bail is one of the two small bars resting on cricket stumps

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the word is turned upwards, read backwards

parts.note: GI Joe is slang for an American soldier, a GI

explanation.surface: A man called Joe is lounging in a little sports bar where a woman serves drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: A bail is one of the two small crosspieces on top of the stumps in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A lady's maid is called by this name in older English, after a servant in a seventeenth-century play.

clue.text: Dandy perhaps stuffs old note in volume

indicators.note: the outer volume letters are packed with the other pieces as filling

parts.note: cc, cubic centimetres, measures volume
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A fop crams an old banknote into a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dandy was a long-running British children's weekly of cartoon strips; 'Dandy' poses as a well-dressed man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dandy was a children's strip-cartoon weekly, an example of a funny paper.

clue.text: Notice books in the 19?

parts.note: to notice something is to spot it
lit is short for literature, books

explanation.surface: A spotter notices a pile of books under the theatre lights.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is LIMELIGHT, Chaplin's 1952 film; being in the limelight means being picked out by a stage light.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in the limelight is lit by a stage beam, as the question mark admits.

clue.text: Black bishop rings Times about Young Conservatives

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: the two rings go about, surrounding, the political letters

parts.note: each ring is a circle, the letter O, so two rings give OO
YC is the abbreviation for the Young Conservatives
T stands for time, so times gives TT

explanation.surface: A newspaper story: a black-clad bishop has Times reporters phoning about Young Conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black' looks like a colour; here it is a verb, to blacklist.
explanation.definitionFit: To blacken or black a firm is to refuse to deal with it, a collective shunning.

clue.text: Ollie nervously hosts northern playwright

indicators.note: the scrambled name takes in a guest letter, holding it inside
doing something nervously is jittery and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A nervous Ollie entertains a dramatist from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nervously' rearranges OLLIE to OEILL, and 'hosts' puts N inside it. Eugene O'Neill's daughter Oona married Chaplin.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill was an American dramatist, author of Long Day's Journey into Night.

clue.text: In the Channel Islands everyone has a duty to arrange transport

indicators.note: the other pieces sit in the island letters, which wrap round them

parts.note: CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands
all means everyone
a duty is a tax on goods

explanation.surface: On Jersey or Guernsey, every citizen must pay a levy towards transport.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands, off the French coast, are known for low taxes, which makes the surface wry.
explanation.definitionFit: Phoning for a cab is the everyday way of organising a ride.

clue.text: Ruler found in school ground

indicators.note: the monarch is discovered sitting inside the other word

parts.note: to school someone is to train them
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A monarch turns up on a school's playing field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' looks like a noun but works as the verb to train.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrain is the lie of the land, a stretch of ground with its features.

clue.text: He wants things just so ropes etc fit in buggy

indicators.note: something buggy is faulty and glitchy, so the letters come out wrong

explanation.surface: A fussy man wants ropes and gear packed neatly into a pushchair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buggy' poses as the pushchair being loaded; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who insists everything be exactly right is a stickler who demands flawlessness.

clue.text: Record first of fifty-one starters for Le Mans

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the starters of words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: A sporting report: fifty-one cars are first to start the Le Mans race.
explanation.definitionFit: To film an event is to capture it on camera, a verb sense of record.

clue.text: A single rock's hiding top lady's shorts

parts.note: a single thing is one

indicators.note: the rocking word conceals the queen inside it

parts.note: to rock is to reel, so rock's gives reels
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen, the top lady

explanation.surface: A lone boulder conceals the knickers of a high-born woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shorts' suggests clothing; here it means short films, apt for Chaplin's early work.
explanation.definitionFit: Short silent films ran to a single reel of film, and Chaplin made many of them.

clue.text: Rogue gunmen's state

parts.note: the RA, Royal Artillery, are gunners, so gunmen's gives RAS
CAL is an abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: A rogue is the condition gunmen find themselves in.
explanation.walkthrough: RA is the Royal Artillery, the British army's gunners.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue is a scamp or scoundrel, someone mischievous or dishonest.

clue.text: Community on holiday like beds in caravans

parts.note: a fold is a flock or congregation, a community of believers
on holiday means away from home

explanation.surface: A community on holiday sleeps in caravans.
explanation.definitionFit: Caravan berths collapse into walls or seats to save space, so they are collapsible by design.

clue.text: Friend's about to tolerate knockabout antics

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word for friends is read backwards

parts.note: pal's, a friend's, gives PALS
to stick something is to put up with it

explanation.surface: A friend is on the verge of putting up with some horseplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical comedy of pratfalls and custard pies is the genre named after a clown's noisy paddle.

clue.text: MC occasionally bears gift after promotion

indicators.note: promotion moves the gift word up, so in this down light it comes first

parts.note: a gift is a present

indicators.note: occasionally means taking only every other letter

explanation.surface: A master of ceremonies sometimes carries a gift after being promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'occasionally' takes the even letters of 'bears', ER; 'after promotion' lifts the word for gift ahead of them.
explanation.definitionFit: An MC, master of ceremonies, is a host who introduces acts on a show.

clue.text: Exponent of 14 fell defending a service

indicators.note: the knockout letters guard the others by surrounding them

parts.note: to fell someone is to knock them out, KO
RN, the Royal Navy, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A man falls while defending a service in tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is SLAPSTICK. Fred Karno ran a British music-hall comedy troupe in which Chaplin and Stan Laurel started.
explanation.definitionFit: Fred Karno was a music-hall impresario whose troupe specialised in knockabout comedy.

clue.text: Tender chest after scrubbing front

indicators.note: scrubbing the front wipes away the opening letter

parts.note: a coffer is a strongbox or chest

explanation.surface: A sore chest after the front of it has been scrubbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like an adjective meaning sore; it is the verb to put forward.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender something is to put it forward formally, as with a bid or a resignation.

clue.text: Pay for a, say, revolting series of frames

parts.note: to foot the bill is to pay for it

indicators.note: revolting means turning over, so the short pieces are read backwards

parts.note: eg, for example, means say

explanation.surface: Someone pays for a disgusting run of pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' poses as disgusting; it reverses EG and A to make AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Film material is a run of frames shot on camera, the stuff of a reel.

clue.text: Writer's Spanish article pricks faint public interest

indicators.note: the pieces pierce the word for faint, ending up inside it

parts.note: light means faint, as in a light touch
the writer of a clue speaks of themself, so writer's is I'm
el is the Spanish word for the

explanation.surface: An author's Spanish article stirs only a little public curiosity.
explanation.walkthrough: Also the title of Chaplin's 1952 film.
explanation.definitionFit: Being the focus of public attention is being in the glare of a stage spotlight.

clue.text: Shed light on old school straddling state borders

parts.note: ex means former, old

indicators.note: to straddle is to sit astride, so the school letters go either side

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins

indicators.note: the borders of a word are its outer letters

explanation.surface: A former school sits astride a state's borders, bringing it to light.
explanation.definitionFit: To shed light on something is to reveal it, uncover it to view.

clue.text: Cleans feet crossing river

indicators.note: the feet go across the river, with its letter inside them

parts.note: hooves are the feet of horses

explanation.surface: Wading across a river cleans the feet.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoover is a vacuum-cleaner brand, used in Britain as a verb for vacuuming.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage to hoover is to vacuum, so this verb means tidies with a vacuum cleaner.

clue.text: Like early 10s, one's rising fast

indicators.note: in a down light, rising means read upwards, backwards

parts.note: one is I, so one's gives IS
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: One is getting up quickly, much like the early versions of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is FILM; early films had no soundtrack.
explanation.definitionFit: Early cinema had no synchronised soundtrack, so its films were speechless.

clue.text: Wag papers etc during trick

indicators.note: the press occurs during the trick, sitting inside it

parts.note: a con is a trick
newspapers and the like are the media

explanation.surface: The press and others wag their tongues during a scam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wag' looks like a verb; it is a noun, a joker.
explanation.definitionFit: A wag is a joker, someone who makes people laugh.

clue.text: Cup-and-ball in past helping child in tavern

parts.note: a pot is a sporting cup, a trophy

indicators.note: the ball sits in the word for past

parts.note: by means past, as in go by
a ball is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: A game of cup-and-ball played in years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: Cup-and-ball is an old toy, a cup on a stick for catching a tethered ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy employed in an inn to fetch and wash tankards was named for the drinking vessels he carried.

clue.text: Stump male in role reversal

indicators.note: the male letter goes in the turned-round word
reversal means the word is read backwards

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

explanation.surface: A man is left baffled when roles are reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stump' is the verb to walk heavily. Chaplin's best-known character is the Little Tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: To stump along is to trudge with heavy steps, which is to march wearily on foot.

clue.text: They clean tables with excellent mops

parts.note: A1 means excellent, read here as the letters AI
mops of hair are tresses

explanation.surface: Cleaners wipe down tables using top-quality mops.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, first-class, has its digit read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Women who serve at restaurant tables also wipe them down between diners.

clue.text: State's mean, cutting time

indicators.note: cutting a piece away removes it from the longer word

parts.note: the mean is the average
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A statistician's state average has been cut back over time.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to declare firmly, to assert something as true.

clue.text: Improved script about western ceremony

parts.note: re means about, concerning
a rite is a ceremony

explanation.surface: A screenplay about a cowboy ceremony has been polished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'western' suggests the film genre; it only gives W.
explanation.definitionFit: To redraft a text is to produce a better version of it.

clue.text: Fatty Arbuckle, initially poised, cracks up

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letter
something that cracks up breaks apart, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The comedian Fatty Arbuckle, at first composed, collapses laughing.
explanation.walkthrough: Roscoe 'Fatty' Arbuckle was a silent-film comedian who worked alongside Chaplin.
explanation.definitionFit: Adipose tissue stores fat in the body, so the word means consisting of fat.
